text: Knowing which failures are retryable is half the job. This lesson builds the actual retry mechanism — exponential backoff with jitter — and the fallback decision logic for when retrying stops being the right call.

Retrying every failure after exactly the same fixed interval sounds reasonable until you realize what happens under provider-side congestion: every client retries in lockstep, making it worse, not better. The fix is exponential backoff with jitter, a real stopping rule, and three fallback options in a specific order of preference.

Here's a real backoff sequence, computed in full. Base delay five hundred milliseconds, doubling each attempt, capped at sixty seconds. Six attempts tops out at thirty-one and a half seconds of total worst-case wait. Full jitter doesn't retry at exactly these numbers — it picks a random delay up to each cap, so many clients hitting the same failure don't all retry at once.

This is a real task run history from Amazon Braket — exactly where retried attempts and their outcomes actually show up over time, which is the evidence your stopping rule needs: a max-attempt count and a cumulative-time budget, combined.

Once you decide to stop retrying, here's fallback option one, and usually the cheapest: retry on a different, available device from this real device list. Option two is falling back to a classical simulator for just that one evaluation, clearly flagged as lower-fidelity. Option three is failing the iteration explicitly, rather than silently substituting a wrong number.
And here's Microsoft's own real diagram of the job states this all plays out across — a failed or cancelled state is exactly where the retry-versus-fallback decision gets made, and logged.
Next lesson assembles everything from this chapter — batching, retry, and fallback — into one complete orchestration design for a hundred fifty-iteration loop that has to survive a genuinely bad day.
